title: Nine Takeaways From Helsinki’s Finnish Film Affair, From Buzzy Titles to Hollywood Whisperers
description: Genre thrills and chills dominated the 15th Finnish Film Affair that closed last night, and splattered across various sections of Helsinki’s Love &
body:
Genre thrills and chills dominated the 15th Finnish Film Affair that closed last night, and splattered across various sections of Helsinki’s Love & Anarchy Film Festival and panel sessions.

	The tone was set with the opening film “Nightborn” by local genre wiz Hanna Bergholm, the inaugural Nordic Genre Lab, and yesterday’s panels about Nordic genre’s market value and positioning, followed by XYZ Films’ masterclass about the morphing of Tommy Wirkola’s “The Trip” into Hollywood’s “Over Your Dead Body.”
	

	“Genre films and series are definitely on the rise, including in Finland where we do have a history of dark, quirky noirs,” said FFA honcho Lydia Taylerson. “When Claire Willats [Two Magpies Entertainment, former Netflix executive] and Laura Laaksonen [Finnish producer, PR expert] approached us with the idea to create a Nordic Genre Lab and use the FFA as a hub, it felt like perfect timing as we wanted to replace Love & Anarchy’s ‘weird’ section, which was a bit vague as a concept,” she said.


	But Nordic fare across all genres – from body horror to kids comedy, dramas and documentaries, showcased at Thursday’s pitch day, played out strongly in Helsinki, based on the positive feedback from industry players such as Mike Runagall, managing director of London-based Altitude Film Sales, who said: “I came eight years ago for a panel. But I now feel that someone from my company should come every year. It’s a real creative hub here,” said the senior sales executive, who plans to track a handful of genre projects.

	Searchlight’s Sydney Brumfield, who was in Helsinki for her Nordic Genre Lab juror duty, concurred. “Finnish Film Affair organizers did an excellent job in selecting the projects because the quality was amazing,” she said.
	

	At last night’s FFA closing speech, Pauliina Ståhlberg, head of the festival thanked all participants, mentors of the training programs Nordic Flair and Nordic Genre Lab, and experts who sat on the 12 panels. “The panels have been great! I’ve learned about what an ‘above-the-line liaison’ does, and why producers should hold on to IP and remake rights. We’ve seen so many different genres. We all need different content at different times of our lives. So let’s help each other tell different stories, about different cultures. At Love and Anarchy, we do believe that with film and TV, with love and anarchy we can make the world a better place,” she said.

	Here is how FFA unrolled in nine takeaways.

	Numbers

	A record 630 attendees signed up for FFA, and 220 meetings between 45 different people were facilitated. At the festival, 121 shorts and 136 films from 80 countries played across the festival’s 20 plus sections. Attendance reached 50,000.

	New boss in town

	On Wednesday Stuba Nikula, the new CEO of the Finnish Film Foundation took the stage and kickstarted the panel sessions. He also sat with Variety and shared good news. On Tuesday, the Finnish government submitted its 2027 budget to Parliament and funding for the local industry via the Finnish Film Foundation should remain stable at €23 million ($26.2 million) a year, he said. Second piece of good news: the industry should soon benefit from much needed extra coin, via the implementation of the EU’s AVMS Directive. Once the law is passed “hopefully within a month,” said Nikula, the money collected from payment obligations for streaming services, set to generate between €3.5 million to €7 million ($4 million to $8 million), will be collected in 2027 and funnelled into the industry in 2028.

	Any lesson from Norway?

	Finns often look with envy at Norway, a country of equal population size as Finland where film support is threefold and funding is matched by regional and equity investors. Yes, the country has a good funding system on a national and regional level, said the Norwegian Film Institute’s rep Kjetil Omberg at a panel. That said, across the Nordics, “public funding is decreasing, deferrals from producers and partners in post is going up, while actual private money is not flowing,” he said, estimating equity funding at only 1% of overall investment in film across the EU. It’s the industry business model based on single project production in the Nordics that needs to change. “People run from one project to the next but don’t build,” he said, urging indie producers to “be more responsible.” “We have to look at the type of stories we make, who sees them. Because it’s also about who is being reached and how. The audience is key.”
	

	What’s up with EU funding?

	The EU’s 35-year-old Media Program comes to an end and audiovisual support will be combined in 2027 with spending for culture, media and civil society under the mega-Agora EU umbrella. It’s now that the industry has to come together and lobby to protect our film infrastructure, urged panellists Hugo Rosak (head of industry at Karlovy Vary) and Julie-Jeanne Regnault (European Producers Club). “Through our training programs, festivals, we contribute to the circulation of films. We do have a solid infrastructure, an eco-system that works, even if sometimes we’re not so good at flagging our success. We need to stick together and make sure the next EU program will be industry-specific to carry the goals and values of EU cinema,” said Rosak.

	Lessons from Hollywood

	How can indie producers make their IP -and coin – go further? At a panel about global franchises moderated by Variety’s Marta Balaga, experts Danny Cannon (“CSI” franchise, “Gotham”), U.K. director/producer, and U.S.-born Jodi Hildebrand (“Marvel,” “Condé Nast”) shared some tips. To make sure viewers keep watching, do create top-tier pilots or first films within franchises, as this is the world in which stories live and where characters eventually go back to, recommended Cannon and Hildebrand. Also, “don’t hold back when you make a pilot – use everything you have, as you never know if you will get other seasons,” said Cannon, who was also in Helsinki to prepare for the Mediawan Nordic noir series “The Faithful Reader,” based on Finnish author Max Seeck’s novels, which he will direct and executive produce.

	Lessons from genre heavyweights

	In today’s shifting market and “new normal” post-COVID, you need to build [your business model] on the floor, not the ceiling, and the new baseline is not theatrical, the transactional window, but ‘Pay1’ i.e. streamers, broadcasters, cable TV where consumers pay for content, said genre expert Todd Brown, former XYZ Films head of acquisitions at a panel. “We’ve been told in film that theatrical, box office is the basis for our economics, but this is a complete utter lie,” he claimed, urging producers to follow the money, where the audience is today – especially Gen Z-online. With SVODs becoming AVODs, we’re reverting to the old broadcast model, so do keep the audience engaged as this is what drives ads,” he said.
	

	Producer Camille Gatin (“The Girl With All the Gifts”) advised producers to stay away from deferments and for genre filmmakers to also think of female audiences. “Women are the ones deciding to go to the movies and they love horror, especially young adults.”

	“Nightborn” helmer Hanna Bergholm praised the co-production model, while Roar Uthaug (“Troll”) said having made blockbuster genre movies in the Norwegian language (“The Wave”) helped open the doors to Hollywood.

	Hit screenings: “Nightborn,” “The Secret Reading Club of Kaboul”

	On the heels of their international festival success, Hanna Bergholm’s horror “Nightborn” and Elina Hirvonen and Shakiba Adil’s documentary “The Secret Reading Club of Kabul” were clear standout titles at Love & Anarchy, ahead of their domestic release. Both scooped Best Nordic Film and Impact Film at Tuesday’s FFA’s preamble, the Freya Nordic film and TV awards and equally wooed Love & Anarchy audiences. At the festival’s official screening attended by Adil and Hirvonen, the documentary about Afghan women received a standing ovation and “there was not a dry eye in the audience,” noted festival chief Ståhlberg. The Finnish-Norwegian documentary has launched a pre-Oscar crowdfunding campaign.

	Ilja Rautsi at the right place

	Back from Austin’s Fantastic film where his “Red Snow” dark comedy world premiered, Ilja Rautsi who also wrote Hanna Bergholm’s “Hatching” and “Nightborn,” said jokingly: “I’m living like in a Monty Python sketch where Michael Palin plays the father who is a playwright and complains to his coal-mining son about attending gala events, saying, you don’t know what real work it!”

	About the genre pics wave, he said, “In Finland we have a history of realistic films and fantasy films for kids. In the past 15 years it’s evolved. I’m proud to be part of this change. I’ve I always loved to use fantasy, horror, sci-fi, genre elements to tell character-driven stories in a gripping way, so I’m in the right time at the right place. It’s a great feeling.”

	Buzz titles

	Among the 38 films and series pitched, besides the FFA winners, standout titles included the Finnish comedy in post-production “The Campers,” Nordic Genre Lab offers “Tick Fever,” “Linden Lane 6,” “Alma,” “Echo Chamber,” “Trespassers” and “Whistler.” Among docs, hot projects were “Mariana’s Lament” and Virpi Suutari’s anticipated “Lonesome Land.”
	

	At the festival, the most popular screenings were “The Samurai and the Prisoner,” “La Bola Negra,” “The History of Concrete,” “The Devils,” “Minotaur,” “Erupcja,” “Arrested Memory,” “No Good Men,” “KitKatClub – Kinks of Berlin” and “Jim Queen.”

title: Mubi CEO Efe Cakerel Praises ‘Incredible’ ‘Primetime’ Opening Weekend: ‘Bold Storytelling Is Here to Stay’
description: Mubi CEO Efe Cakarel praised Lance Oppenheim’s “Primetime” while in a rare public appearance at the Zurich Summit. Talking about the phenomenon of y
body:
Mubi CEO Efe Cakarel praised Lance Oppenheim’s “Primetime” while in a rare public appearance at the Zurich Summit. Talking about the phenomenon of young audiences returning to cinemas, the exec said that when he hears about a $20 million opening weekend for a film like Oppenheim’s Venice hit, it is “incredible.”

	“You look at the demographic of who’s watching this story, which you would think appeals to an older audience, and it’s incredibly healthy—the younger audiences who are watching,” he added. “I think the experience of watching a film, watching original, bold storytelling is here to stay, and it’s gonna grow. We as an industry need to embrace it. We need to continue to produce and finance these films. We need to try to find their audiences because they exist. It’s not huge. It’s not the majority of the households, but it’s meaningful enough for us to continue doing what we love.”
	

	Cakarel brought up his 14-year-old son, who lives in Geneva and travelled to watch his dad speak on stage but dodged the idea of a family dinner in favor of watching Kane Parsons’ “Backrooms” in the cinema with a post-screening Q&A. “That is profound. And that is also the reason why you started to see the box-office success over the past 24 months—a lot of this independent, bold storytelling.”


	The exec also spoke about being in the same room as one of his “heroes,” Oscar-winning director Edward Berger. Cakarel brought up the “Conclave” helmer when talking about a desire to grow his company.

	“I started Mubi 19 years ago,” he noted. “It took us 15 years to get to a place where you could start imagining being able to finance a film by Paweł Pawlikowski,” he said, referring to the Cannes-winning “Fatherland.”
	

	“In 15 years, we went from zero to 40 employees and then, in the past four years, we went from 40 to more than 400,” continued the exec. “But it took 15 years of putting together brick by brick this vision. Everything takes a long time. You just need to have a vision and stick with it—that’s my resilience formula.”

	Growth, for Cakarel, is not “for the sake of ambition,” or having “more and more.” “It is just to be able to do the things that you want to do. If you want to be able to greenlight and fully finance an Edward Berger film and release it, distribute it globally, you need the capital and also capabilities to do that. And the goal for us was to get to that place as soon as possible, but not sooner.”

	“The road to growth and success is never a straight line [because] when you are growing really fast, sometimes growth hides a lot of problems,” he said, before adding that 2023 and 2024 were “phenomenal years at Mubi,” whereas 2025 was “slower.” “This year, again, incredible. The idea is not just grow, grow, grow. Become big, big, big.”

	Cakarel recalled growing up in a small Mediterranean city on the West Coast of Turkey. “There was a beautiful arthouse cinema that my mom used to take me to. That’s how I fell in love with films,” he said, before mentioning how his 20-year-old sister, who still lives in that same town, needs to rely on “multiplexes in shopping centers” for entertainment. “It’s mostly really big, IP-based, you know, blockbusters, right?”

	“Over the past 20 years, we saw this significant decline of the kind of films that we represent not being exposed, not being distributed, because it’s just very difficult to reach audiences,” he continued. “There’s this whole era of TikToks and so on and so forth, where we are just so addicted to immediate short-form content.”

	As he “thinks about the future,” what Cakarel is observing is that younger audiences “are actually quite discerning.” “They are not easily fooled, and they seek high-quality entertainment in a world where they can reach anything, and they really value experiences.”

title: Nas, Jeremy Pope, Ashlee Simpson and More Toast Krug’s New Champagne-and-Sound Experience at L.A.’s Larrabee Studios

body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Krug is pairing Champagne with live music at Larrabee Studios.

	The luxury Champagne house is opening the doors to one of Los Angeles’ most storied recording studios this month for “The Art of Blending Krug & Sound,” a three-night experience at Larrabee Studios that will turn guests’ tasting notes — or, more precisely, whatever memories, emotions and sensations their Champagne inspires — into an original song created in real time.


	The experience will take place Sept. 28-30 inside Larrabee’s Studio 6, with 14-time Grammy-winning mixing engineer and studio owner Manny Marroquin (who most recently worked on Rosalía’s highly lauded “LUX”) leading the experiment alongside producers Scott Tibbs, Nick Rosen and Mike Bennett. Rather than simply putting on a playlist while everyone drinks, the producers will use guests’ reactions to each pour as raw material for a composition assembled live over the course of the evening.



	

					Problem, Manny Marroquin
									Kyle Goldberg/BFA.com
	





	

									Kyle Goldberg/BFA.com
	





	

									Kyle Goldberg/BFA.com
	



	At the center of the evening are Krug 2013 and Krug Grande Cuvée 169ème Édition, while Chef Oscar Torres of VERSE will serve a multi-course dinner paired with additional pours including Krug Grande Cuvée 173ème Édition and Krug Rosé 29ème Édition.

	“Larrabee has always been a place where creativity comes to life through exchange,” Marroquin said. “Partnering with Krug gave us the opportunity to invite guests into that process, where every conversation, every shared moment and every glass of Champagne becomes part of the music we’re creating together. No two evenings will ever be the same.”


	The public run was preceded Thursday night by a splashier VIP preview, where Nas, Ashlee Simpson Ross, Evan Ross, Jeremy Pope, Sabrina Claudio, producer Dahi, pianist Chloe Flower and others gathered inside Studio 6 to test-drive the concept before it opens to paying guests.

	Over the course of the evening, guests sipped through the Krug lineup and wrote down emotions, sensations and words each cuvée brought to mind, which Tibbs, Rosen and Costa then translated into an original composition created live in the room. Words like “red,” “invigorating,” and “nostalgia” informed two lively songs played on cello, piano and drums. 



	

					Chloe Flower
									Kyle Goldberg/BFA.com
	



	In between, the studio played tracks with their own Larrabee history, including John Mayer’s “Gravity” and Portugal. The Man’s “Feel It Still.” The finale came courtesy of Flower, who surprised the room with a live piano performance as a jeroboam of Krug Grande Cuvée 163ème Édition was brought out for one last pour.

	The collaboration isn’t entirely out of left field for Krug. The Champagne house has long experimented with the relationship between music and taste, working with musicians and composers — most recently Max Richter — to explore how sound can affect perception and emotion while drinking. 

	And if drinking Krug inside a recording studio sounds suspiciously like the kind of night normally reserved for people with a platinum record on the wall, that’s part of the draw. The intimate sessions offer rare public access to Studio 6, with a limited number of reservations available through Tock.

	After the three-night run wraps, the collaboration will spill over into Larrabee’s neighboring restaurants VERSE and Mensano, where Torres will offer a month-long Krug Grande Cuvée pairing inspired by the project.

	Find out more about “The Art of Blending Krug & Sound” here.

title: Author Chloe Gong on ‘Eyes of Kings’ ending, ‘Deadlock’ debut and how she wants ‘These Violent Delights’ adapted for TV or film
description: Chloe Gong has had a busy 2026. The author best known for her hit 2020 “Romeo & Juliet” retelling “These Violent Delights,” which is set in 1920s Sh
body:
Chloe Gong has had a busy 2026. The author best known for her hit 2020 “Romeo & Juliet” retelling “These Violent Delights,” which is set in 1920s Shanghai, released the conclusion of one trilogy series last month and is preparing for the launch of her second book in another series in November, all while writing two more books to debut in the coming years.

	“I’m currently working on the final book in ‘The StrangeLoom’ trilogy,” Gong told Variety in a late August interview, not long after the Aug. 4 release of “Eyes of Kings,” the final book in her “Flesh & False Gods” saga. “It is always really strange to talk about because ‘Deadlock‘ isn’t out yet. That’s coming out in November, but already I’m deep in the weeds of getting that third and final book finished and I’m very excited about how that’s going to look. I always love writing the final book in a trilogy because it’s so explosive and there’s so much in the world to figure out, but does it kill me a little every time? Absolutely. I’m currently working on that. I’m also in the revision process of a secret project that we haven’t yet announced, but I hope too soon and I always feel like, as authors, there’s so many secrets that we’re hiding until we’re suddenly not hiding it and they’re like, please, let me tell you about this book that I have coming out.”
	

	With “Deadlock,” the sequel to 2025’s “Coldwire,” set for a Nov. 17 release and the currently untitled third book in the works, Gong is balancing that project with a top-secret book that isn’t a return to the “These Violent Delights” universe or any of her previous series.
	

	“It’s secret because it’s brand new for me. It’s my first venture into something contemporary,” Gong says, “I have been kind of teasing it as, imagine an Emily Henry love story meets the zombie apocalypse. I’m super excited to talk about it more, and I think at this point, I’ve done that teaser enough times that I’m like, it’s OK, my publisher’s not gonna sack me for that.”

	Amid her packed writing schedule, Gong has taken some time to view readers’ reactions to the end of “Eyes of Kings” — the final installment in her trilogy inspired by Shakespeare’s “Antony and Cleopatra” — but she says she’s not actively seeking out fans’ hot takes.

	“I don’t look it up with my own volition,” Gong says. “I like to save my sanity that way, but I have some amazing readers who will tag me in their reactions. They will tag me in their crying videos, or they’ll tag me in their Instagram pictures where they have these beautiful aesthetic flat lays and the captions are like ‘Chloe Gong, how dare you!’ I love those reactions, especially when it comes to the end of the series. I have been preparing people, I think from Book 1. I’m like, guys, this is adult epic fantasy, I’m not promising to go light on you and there’s a fight coming. And the very tagline of ‘Eyes of Kings’ is, ‘At the end of this war, there can only be one king.’ I’ve been bracing everyone, I think. I’ve loved the reader reactions. You know, no one’s happy, but everyone’s had a great time, I think.”

	While Gong’s projects have yet to be adapted for the big screen, a project based on “These Violent Delights” has been rumored for some time and Gong says there’s still potential for it to move forward.

	“As far as I know, things are always moving somehow in the industry,” Gong says. “But I don’t have anything to report, at least as of now. People are always looking at my work. People are considering, and people are in conversation. And I always have my fingers crossed that something will come of it. At least for what I can focus on, I just try to write the books that would look good and feel fun and be exciting to adapt, but my focus is on the words on the page and I can just hope that someone who shares the vision would see the visual equivalent.”

	Gong says she is very open to collaboration and the changes that can come with adapting a book for TV or film.
	

	“I’ve always said I would love any type of adaptation. I’m such an unfussy author,” Gong says. “I probably have the least amount of opinions ever when it comes to what an adaptation would look like, because I just think it would be so cool to have one at all. I think fantasy is a terrain that is quite hard to adapt. There’s so much CGI involved, especially when you have characters doing effectively what is magic, even though I don’t use that term in the series. There are so many cool things that I think would be great on a screen. It just depends on who wants to do it. So Hollywood, call me.”

title: ‘Ghost Song’ Review: Fatih Akin Doesn’t Find Top Form in This Supernatural Romance, but at Least It Has Beautiful Ghosts
description: Since hitting an artistic peak with the back-to-back festival triumphs “Head-On” and “Edge of Heaven” in the mid-2000s, German-Turkish auteur Fatih
body:
Since hitting an artistic peak with the back-to-back festival triumphs “Head-On” and “Edge of Heaven” in the mid-2000s, German-Turkish auteur Fatih Akin has darted all over the map in genre, style and form — occasionally striking commercially, as with the Diane Kruger thriller “In the Fade” and the local hip-hop biopic “Rhinegold,” without ever matching the rigor and impact of those earlier standouts. That pattern doesn’t change with his latest, the star-crossed supernatural romance “Ghost Song,” which opened this year’s San Sebastian Film Festival. The film, about two 20-year-olds carrying on their early courtship across the mortal divide, is earnest and a little clunky as it takes a simplistic inspirational approach to complex metaphysical questions. But it is accessible and attractive, shot in glistening monochrome, and could well be a youth-skewing hit for the filmmaker.
	

	The choice to shoot in inky black-and-white, making prominent use of major German city landmarks, practically begs for comparisons to Wim Wenders’ “Wings of Desire,” another atmospheric romantic fantasy about a love spanning the mortal and ethereal realms — with Akin’s film the Hamburg-set, GenZ-focused homage to Wenders’ Berlin classic. Placing the two side by side doesn’t flatter the thinner, less lyrical new work, but it’s a marketable resemblance, while “Ghost Song” asserts its own identity with an expression of Muslim faith, as interrogated and interpreted by its young, multicultural characters. The fact that “Ghost Song” has simultaneously been adapted into a graphic novel by Akin and artist Bea Davies is a further indication of its generational targeting.
	

	Farasha (luminous first-timer Mariam Dawoud) is a Syrian refugee who has settled and assimilated in Hamburg with her family, following an interstitial stint in Turkey. Though she chooses to wear a traditional headscarf, in other respects she lives as a modern, independent-minded woman, following in the footsteps of her late father by studying physics at university, while keeping at least one haram secret that would scandalize her mother: a butterfly tattoo on her stomach. 

	At a graduation party in Hamburg’s imposing Telemichel tower, she meets and immediately sparks with fellow grad Faris (Eren M. Guvercin), a tousle-haired, German-born Muslim of Turkish descent. With her very tipsy bestie Una (Carlotta von Falkenhayn), they decide to continue the party elsewhere and pile into his car; in circumstances deliberately (and somewhat luridly) parceled out over the course of the film, an accident sees the vehicle plunge into the Elbe river.

	Faris wakes up in hospital to find that Farasha has drowned, and the police have questions; Farasha, meanwhile, comes to in a different way, finding that she can still walk the Earth, but no one can see or hear her. No one, that is, except her father, who informs her that for 40 days — in line with the mourning period in certain Muslim traditions — she can visit the living in their dreams. Still lovestruck and not yet fully accepting of her death, she seizes the opportunity to spend more time with Faris, cuing a strange and increasingly dangerous courtship.

	“Ghost Song” rests on the idea that, in just one evening, Farasha and Faris made such a deep soul connection that even death can’t quite sever them. It’s an intensely romantic notion not really borne out by these wan characters, however individually charismatic the young actors playing them. Nor by Akin’s naïve, slightly purple writing, which keeps sentimentally reiterating the characters’ devotion to each other — mining tension from the question of which will ultimately make the biggest sacrifice for the other — but says little of any spiritual or philosophical substance. More moving is the film’s observation of Farasha’s family through this nightmare: A literal out-of-body scene in which she watches them ritually clean and prepare her corpse for burial is the film’s most layered and haunting.
	

	Where the film veers into the superficial or kitsch, however, it can fall back on its lush mood and widescreen visual riches. Being a ghost has rarely looked quite this pretty on screen, as Tom Tykwer’s regular DP Frank Griebe — working for the first time with Akin — makes a chiaroscuro lovers’ playground of even Hamburg’s unlovelier spots, finding as much intimacy in a brutalist monument as an ordinary darkened bedroom. Iridescently illustrated title cards disrupt the stark monochrome, as do the moments leading into the closing credits — the characters’ worlds flooding into color with a crucial, life-or-death choice.

title: Finnish Hit ‘100 Litres of Gold’ Gets Another Round With Sequel ‘200 Litres of Gold’ That’s a ‘Little Bit Darker, a Little Bit Funnier and a Little Bit Bigger’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Box-office hit “100 Litres of Gold” – last year’s Finnish Oscar submission – is getting a sequel, downing additional “200 Litres of Gold” as the boo
body:
Box-office hit “100 Litres of Gold” – last year’s Finnish Oscar submission – is getting a sequel, downing additional “200 Litres of Gold” as the boozy saga about Finnish beer sahti continues.

	“In the first one, the sisters were making sahti for their sister’s wedding. Now, they are making it for the Finnish Sahti Championship. To win, they need to tolerate each other and overcome rival sahti makers – and their father,” says director Teemu Nikki.
	

	“Needless to say, things don’t go too smoothly, resulting in physical and mental damage.”


	Obviously, no one’s going to stay sober for long. But the comedy also stems from other sources, and the relationships between the sisters, and their father, are “even more complex than before,” says Nikki.

	There’s also a new nemesis in town: the sahti makers from another village.

	“They are two ladies who are as crazy as our sisters. There’s a lot of trash-talking and arm-wrestling.”

	Elina Knihtilä and Pijo Lonka return as Pirkko and Taina.

	“They’re close, for sure. But how well they’re able to take on life’s challenges, both together and alone, is part of the story’s theme,” notes Lonka.

	“Actors have to find a way to love the characters they play, and these women were easy to love. They’re human. They’re not one-dimensional; they’re vulnerable, flawed and sometimes childlike. But with all their imperfections, you can relate to them and grow close to them.”

	It was liberating to get a role like that, she says.

	“It doesn’t happen very often for women. It’s great to show such a wide spectrum of emotions without holding back, and the person to thank for that is Teemu.”
	

	“100 Litres of Gold” has already made waves abroad, with Dennis Lehane working on a U.S. remake.

	Nikki and producer Jani Pösö are no beginners – with their production company It’s Alive Films, they have already created the likes of “The Blind Man Who Did Not Want to See Titanic,” awarded in Venice, or their first Oscar submission “Euthanizer.” They’re also behind Naima Mohamud’s “Halima.”

	However, no other film has come close to the box-office results of “100 Litres of Gold,” the most-watched local film in 2025.

	“It still feels a bit strange that it did so well. It’s like we kept on hitting our heads against a wall until it finally collapsed,” laughs Pösö.

	“In a way, I think we’ve become better filmmakers. Everything just clicked, from marketing and distribution to acting. Elina has been with us since the very first short we made, she has been fantastic in every role, and we finally got to work with Pirjo.”

	They are happy to see this unlikely franchise grow.

	“We are not sequel guys. But Teemu said: ‘I’m thinking of this as ‘The Godfather,’ and ‘The Godfather Part II’ was better than the first one,’” jokes Pösö.

	“It’s a little bit darker, a little bit funnier and a little bit bigger. We find out that one of the sisters is not doing great; her liver has basically exploded. As in all our films, things get pretty serious in the end, even though it’s fun. It’s also totally independent, so you can watch it without having seen the first one. But the second one will make you want to watch the first one, and vice versa,” he says.

	“With all franchises, there comes a moment when you need to stop. But a third one is certainly possible.”

title: ‘Obsession,’ ‘Backrooms’ Ushering in Shift Similar to ‘Easy Rider’ in 1970s, Sony Pictures Classics Co-Chief Says
description: There has not been a single major industry event in the last three months where major producers and execs have not brought up the phenomenon of Kane
body:
There has not been a single major industry event in the last three months where major producers and execs have not brought up the phenomenon of Kane Parsons’ “Backrooms” and Curry Barker’s “Obsession.” The two films, directed by 20-something-year-olds who came from YouTube, exploded all box-office expectations while ushering in droves of Gen Z audiences back to cinemas. As the industry rushes to try to understand how to capitalize on that momentum, Parsons is already looking ahead.
	

	The young director, who is already working on the sequel to the $400 million grossing A24 film, told an audience of industry insiders at Zurich Summit on Saturday that he didn’t direct the adaptation of his own YouTube analog web series as a “horror film.” “I don’t view it as a horror project. I think that’s just naturally in the path of least resistance from a marketing perspective and is what seems comfortable to people as a framing device.”


	“I’m gonna try to stay as oblivious to those labels as possible,” he added. “I think I have more creative control now with future projects. So those sort of structures will probably be a little less forceful, I think, in the future.”

	Speaking of sequels, fellow Zurich Summit panellist Robbie Brenner, president and chief content officer at Mattel Studios, was asked about a possible sequel to Greta Gerwig’s smash hit “Barbie.” Her answer was brief but positive: “Look, we all wanna have a ‘Barbie’ sequel. I mean, who doesn’t wanna see the sequel to ‘Barbie’? And I’m sure at some point in time there will be one. We all want it to happen. We’ll see.”
	

	Young maverick Parsons stood as the spokesperson for his generation in a panel next to industry titans: Brenner as well as Michael Barker, co-president of Sony Pictures Classics, and Bill Kramer, CEO of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. Parsons said he did not want to make it “too much of an age thing” but that there is a clear “appetite” for the theatrical experience at the moment.

	Parsons believes audiences see “Backrooms” as a “pre-existing but decentralized IP presence online” and he thinks “people are looking for that newness, that sort of detachment from more cyclical cultural icons that keep eating themselves.”

	Kramer jumped in to say how “Backrooms” was an amazing example of fandoms travelling from YouTube to cinemas. “It was the first time that we saw [that].”

	“Young people want to go back to movie theaters,” he added. “Fandoms shift; theatrical can inform a fandom, YouTube can inform a theatrical fandom. It’s all connected in a way that I don’t think we thought was possible. And that, for me, was a big takeaway of this summer. And it gives me great hope for the film industry because we’re seeing young people come back to the movies, and that’s really key.”

	When Parsons brought up the notion that people around his age “gravitate toward short-form material,” Kramer intercepted to say it is “reductive,” to which the director said: “Yes, it is reductive.”

	“Young people want to go back to movie theaters. Fandoms shift; theatrical can inform a fandom, YouTube can inform a theatrical fandom. It’s all connected in a way that I don’t think we thought was possible. And that, for me, was a big takeaway of this summer. And it gives me great hope for the film industry because we’re seeing young people come back to the movies, and that’s really key.”

	“I feel like the sentiment is more that this is weaponized. This algorithmically incentivized [reality] is not really something I think most people enjoy about their own wiring. They don’t love that their attention spans are being sucked into the spiral of mostly consuming stuff that is that short. Going into a closed room without outsider interference […] lowers the tempo in a way that is refreshing.”

	Barker compared the “Obsession” and “Backrooms” summer to the industry shift caused by Dennis Hopper’s “Easy Rider” in the 70s. “‘Easy Rider’ came out in the middle of the Vietnam War, in the middle of a right-wing presidency. It spoke to young people; they responded in huge numbers, and it affected the movies that were gonna be made afterwards.”
	

	“I think this is that moment, this summer with ‘Obsession’ and ‘Backrooms,’” he said.

	Kramer also spoke about YouTube, especially the multi-year agreement that grants the online platform exclusive global rights to stream the Oscars live and free worldwide. The deal will begin in 2029 and run through 2033.

	Asked if it was a good deal, the CEO smiled and said: “A very good deal. We are a nonprofit, so this also allows us to sustain our great work,” he added.

schema.headline: ‘Obsession,’ ‘Backrooms’ Ushering in Shift Similar to ‘Easy Rider’ in 1970s, Sony Pictures Classics Co-Chief Says

title: Naima Mohamud Explains Why Finland Needs a Film Like ‘Halima’: ‘It Was a Long Time Coming’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Finnish-Somali director Naima Mohamud’s debut feature, “Halima,” was named Best Fiction Project at the Finnish Film Affair.

	It’s not the first awa
body:
Finnish-Somali director Naima Mohamud’s debut feature, “Halima,” was named Best Fiction Project at the Finnish Film Affair.

	It’s not the first award for the film, which has consistently generated buzz also outside of the country. But it’s the first Finnish feature film directed by a Black woman.

	Produced by It’s Alive Films, No-Office Films and Vico Films and currently in post-production, it’s set in 1998 in Finland. Halima is a 10-year-old imaginative Somali girl who’s obsessed with Leonardo DiCaprio and Aqua (the band behind hit “Barbie Girl”), and wants nothing more than to be a pop star. The only trouble is, her family is always on the move, she has never had a friend and her mom refuses to talk about her dad.
	

	“To be honest, I really think that a film like ‘Halima’ was a long time coming. We Somalis have been living in Finland for over 35 years, yet most Finns still don’t know anything about us, our culture or how we interact at home. None of those things,” Mohamud tells Variety.

	“This film might help someone with a Somali neighbor finally get a glimpse. I hope that’s what this film does: opens up Finns to understanding Somalis.”

	But Halima, who’s all about pop, is an outsider also in her own family.

	“She has all these dreams of becoming a big star, which confuses her mom. She gets in trouble at school because of her imagination, and her mom just can’t understand the dancing and obsession with music. But she has bigger fish to fry, she has to support the family and make sure everyone’s okay, so she accepts it in her own way.”
	

	Other kids aren’t that forgiving. Luckily, Halima is still young enough not to listen to haters – for now.

	“She loves Lene, the lead singer of Aqua and she wants her bangs. Her hair is different, so when she cuts it, of course it looks weird. She’s okay with it, though, until other kids start bullying her,” says Mohamud.

	“She’s still a child who’s not too self-conscious, but she’s slowly starting to understand that maybe this is embarrassing? Maybe I really look horrible?”



	

	



	Some directors find it hard to see things from a child’s perspective. But not Mohamud.

	“I’m still a kid!,” she laughs.

	“I’ve always understood kids, so I had a great time working with them. I really enjoy this innocence of childhood. The older you get, the more you overthink. You start doubting yourself too much. Kids don’t have that. Halima thinks she can dance, and in her mind, she’s brilliant. When I decided to become a filmmaker at 14, I also didn’t think it was impossible – or that it would take so many years.”

	She adds: “I like that ‘childish’ way of thinking, that everything is possible. You want something, and you go for it. I was just a very curious kid, too. I’d wonder: ‘Would my backpack fit in the school mailbox? What would it feel like to jump out of the window in the middle of class and roll around in the snow? Let’s find out!”

	She wants to give Halima a moment of triumph in the film.

	“There’s triumph, but it’s mischievous,” smiles Mohamud, whose goal is to make “joyful films.”

	“I like happiness, and I like feeling happy. I love watching deep, serious films the same way I love looking at beautiful pieces of art. But I don’t want to spend my time making them,” she admits.

	“It’s so important to know who you are as a filmmaker. I’ll just give you an example: recently, I wrote a short film about a reclusive Muslim scholar who’s asked to wash the dead body of a stranger who died alone. The experience helps her heal her own grief. It’s a very serious film, and I knew I could never direct it.” 

	“Camphor” will be directed by Ayla Amano.

	“That film needed a poetic soul, and that’s not me – at least not as a director. I’d probably make the characters tell a few jokes and it would be so inappropriate. Even in film school, my classmates were all about the French New Wave. I loved James Cameron,” she admits.
	

	“It’s just who I am, and I’m not going to change. I make films that I hope make you feel good when you leave the cinema. A tear here or there is great, but at the end, I want people to say: ‘You know what? Life is amazing.’”

schema.headline: Naima Mohamud Explains Why Finland Needs a Film Like ‘Halima’: ‘It Was a Long Time Coming’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘The Last of Us’ Season 3 Casts John Goodman, Video Game Stars Laura Bailey and Ian Alexander
description:
Actor John Goodman and video game stars Laura Bailey and Ian Alexander will be added to the Season 3 cast of HBO drama “The Last of Us.” 

	Goodman
body:
Actor John Goodman and video game stars Laura Bailey and Ian Alexander will be added to the Season 3 cast of HBO drama “The Last of Us.” 

	Goodman plays Joey, one half of the self-nicknamed “Heroes of the Highway” duo from the series based on a Sony PlayStation video game series that follows characters in postapocalyptic America. “The Last of Us,” led by showrunner and executive producer Craig Mazin, is expected to return to HBO next year for what may be its final season.
	

	Alexander steps into the role of Paco, the other half of the duo. Alexander previously played Lev in “The Last of Us: Part II” video game. The actor also appeared in “The OA” television series as Buck Vu.


	Bailey portrays Elizabeth, one of the leaders of the Seraphites religious sect. Bailey played Abby in “The Last of Us: Part II” video game. She has also lent her voice to “The Legend of Vox Machina” series and the 2023 “Spider-Man 2” video game as Mary Jane Watson.

	Previously announced new cast members for Season 3 are Clea Duvall, Patrick Wilson, Jason Ritter, Jorge Lendeborg Jr., Michelle Mao and Kyriana Kratter.

	Returning cast for the season includes Kaitlyn Dever, Bella Ramsey, Isabella Merced, Gabriel Luna and Jeffrey Wright. Ariela Barer, Tati Gabrielle and Spencer Lord have been promoted to series regular for Season 3.

	Goodman plays President Compson in the highly anticipated movie “Digger,” starring Tom Cruise, which opens Oct. 2.

	Goodman is represented by Gersh. Alexander is represented by Curate. Bailey is represented by CAA.
	

	“The Last of Us,” based on the hit video game franchise of the same name, takes place in a world hit by a widespread infection that has turned most of the population into zombielike creatures.

	The series was cocreated by Mazin and game creator Neil Druckmann. It was previously announced that Druckmann was exiting the show ahead of Season 3, and Mazin will be sole showrunner for the season in addition to writing and executive producing. The series is co-produced by HBO and Sony Pictures Television and executive produced by Carolyn Strauss, Jacqueline Lesko, Cecil O’Connor, Asad Qizilbash, Carter Swan and Evan Wells. PlayStation Productions, Word Games, Mighty Mint and Naughty Dog produce.

	(Pictured: Laura Bailey, John Goodman, Ian Alexander)

            Good news for Carrot Top ... the comedian has been released from the hospital and is feeling better, TMZ has confirmed.
      
    
            A source with direct knowledge tells us ... Carrot is now at "home with his family and doing well." PEOPLE was first to report the news.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Our source also tells us ... Carrot is communicating and talking with his family.
      
    
            As TMZ first reported ... Carrot attempted suicide and was in critical condition after authorities received a call for a "suspected overdose" at his Las Vegas home on September 18.
      

            According to a police report, obtained by TMZ, cops responded to the scene and discovered Carrot — breathing but unconscious -- next to a pool in his backyard.
      
    
            The report says Carrot’s manager had informed him about a published news article, stating that Carrot had been sexually inappropriate.
      
    
            Carrot responded by saying that his show was going to be over ... and he hoped a third party and her daughter would be “okay without him,” according to police.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Carrot then allegedly texted the manager, saying he was “Done.” Police say the manager couldn't get back in touch with Carrot, so he contacted the authorities to go to Carrot's home.
      
    
            A woman who went to check on Carrot also called 911, and you can hear her frantic voice on dispatch audio saying that Carrot was awake but "passing out," with his eyes rolling back and his face turning blue. 
      
    
            Carrot was then rushed to the hospital, where he remained until recently.
      
    
            If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat 988lifeline.org.
